title: US House Passes Sweeping Restrictions on Lawmaker Stock Trading
excerpt: The 'Stop Insider Trading Act' cleared the House 232-198, barring lawmakers and their families from buying new stocks while in office, though a voter ID provision attached to the bill drew fierce Democratic opposition.
body:
• The House passed the Stop Insider Trading Act with a vote of 232-198, implementing significant restrictions on lawmaker stock trading.
  • Lawmakers and their families are prohibited from purchasing new stocks while in office, and selling requires advance notice of 7 to 14 days.
  • A voter ID provision attached to the bill led to opposition from most Democrats, complicating bipartisan support.
  • The bill's future in the Senate is uncertain, as it requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster.
Key Takeaways
  • The House passed the Stop Insider Trading Act 232-198, marking a significant reform since 2012.
  • Lawmakers and families are barred from buying new stocks while in office; selling requires advance notice.
  • A voter ID provision attached to the bill caused most Democrats to oppose it.
  • The bill's future in the Senate is uncertain, needing 60 votes to overcome a filibuster.
  • 83% of Americans support restrictions on lawmaker stock trading, highlighting public concern.

What the Bill Does

The House on Wednesday approved the Stop Insider Trading Act, a sweeping package that restricts — but does not fully ban — stock trading by members of Congress. The bill passed 232 to 198, according to CNN, with every Republican and 13 Democrats voting in favor.

https://x.com/cryptorover/status/2080041950326260138

Under the legislation, lawmakers, their spouses, and dependent children are prohibited from purchasing individual stocks of publicly traded companies while serving in Congress. They can still retain stocks already owned before entering office, buy private stocks, and maintain certain investment funds, according to CNN.

Selling existing stock holdings would require filing public notice 7 to 14 days in advance. Violations carry a penalty of $2,000 or 10% of the transaction's value — whichever is greater — plus forfeiture of any profits from the trade, CNN reported.

"I believe it is time we just stop allowing members to buy new stock. Doing so removes the appearance of impropriety altogether."

— Bryan Steil, GOP Chairman, House Administration Committee

Voter ID Provision Splits the Vote

What could have been a bipartisan win turned partisan after Republican leadership attached a voter ID requirement to the stock trading bill. The provision mandates photo identification for all voters, including those casting mail-in ballots — a dealbreaker for most Democrats.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called the combination "a GOP effort to sabotage national mail-in voting, disguised as a trading ban," according to the New York Post. Democratic Rep. Seth Magaziner, who co-led a stalled bipartisan bill to fully ban stock trading, told CNN that Republicans were "trying to trick members into supporting" voter suppression by linking it to a popular reform.

Even Republican Rep. Thomas Massie acknowledged the maneuver. "Republicans added voter-ID in the legislation. Not to get Dems to vote for voter-ID, but to get them to vote against the stock trading ban, so they can use it in the Nov. election," he wrote on X, according to Fox News.

Thirteen Democrats crossed party lines to support the bill: Reps. Kathy Castor, Henry Cuellar, Don Davis, Jared Golden, Vicente Gonzalez, Josh Gottheimer, Marcy Kaptur, Susie Lee, Jared Moskowitz, Chris Pappas, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, Darren Soto, and Derek Tran, the New York Post reported.

Who Trades the Most on Capitol Hill

Data from Quiver Quantitative, cited by the New York Post, reveals the scale of congressional stock trading that prompted the legislation. Indian American Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) tops the list, with his household executing 4,772 trades totaling $65.9 million last year. Khanna has maintained that the investments are managed by a third-party trustee through a trust set up by his in-laws before his marriage.

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's household made $52.5 million in trades across 21 occasions. Rep. Michael McCaul's (R-Texas) family moved $48 million across 980 trades. The data underscores a longstanding public concern: a 2025 Pew Research poll found 83% of Americans support restrictions on lawmaker stock trading.

A Long Road Through the Senate

The bill's prospects in the Senate remain uncertain. It requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, and the voter ID provision makes Democratic support unlikely in its current form. Fox News reported that Republican Rep. Zach Nunn expressed hope it could reach President Trump's desk before the August recess, but analysts say the packaging makes that improbable.

Democrats have argued the bill does not go far enough. Rep. Joe Morelle, the top Democrat on the elections oversight committee, said the legislation fails to extend trading restrictions to the president, vice president, and federal judicial officers, according to Fox News. A bipartisan bill to fully ban lawmaker stock trading was introduced in September 2025 but has stalled, CNN reported.

"For too long, Americans have watched politicians enrich themselves while asking the public to trust them. That has to end."

— Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas)

What It Means for Diaspora Investors

The legislation carries particular resonance for Indian American professionals in finance and tech who watch congressional trading patterns. With Indian American lawmakers like Khanna among the top traders by volume, the reforms spotlight the intersection of personal wealth management and public service. For NRI investors who follow congressional stock disclosures as market signals — a practice that has spawned an entire cottage industry of "Congress trading" trackers — the advance notice requirement for stock sales could reshape how these disclosures are used.

The bill represents the most significant attempt to reform congressional stock trading since the STOCK Act of 2012, which created disclosure requirements but failed to curb the practice. Whether the Senate takes it up, strips the voter ID provision to attract bipartisan support, or lets it languish remains the central question heading into the August recess.
